title: Into the Eagle's Nest
build: PAL cassette, Pandora, inlay stamped 1986, analysed at the loader's hand-over

records.c: the processor port's direction register, which the KERNAL sets to $2F and the game leaves alone

the processor port. The game uses $36 in play; $26, the same banking, when it leaves play for the lift, a delivered prisoner or a destroyed castle ($48D4, $49EC, $4A5C); $37 when it wants every ROM; $35, the KERNAL out and the I/O in, while it copies the plaque's colours from $EE00 and $EF00 ($0BCA, $0F57); $30 when the map builder reads the floor descriptions under the I/O area; and $00, all RAM, for a moment at $6E89.

the low byte of the map address being read or written. $51CD works it out for a tile lookup from $02B6 and $02B7 and the room's place in $FA and $FB; the map builder sets it at $6A6B and steps it through the castle map as it writes, and the tile fade at $4CCB points it into the character set at $2000 instead.
the high byte of that place
the low byte of the map builder's source, the block it is copying from; the tile fade at $4CCB uses the same pair as its pointer into the copy of the character set it keeps at $8000
the high byte of that pointer: the map builder's source block, or the tile fade's place in its copy at $8000
the low byte of the place the tile grid is read from

the high byte of the place the six-by-six tile grid is read from, which $5C55 steps up twice and back down twice to reach the six rows (0, 2 and 4, then 5, 3 and 1); the door openers ($50F7) and the grid write-back ($4E77) use the same pointer
the low byte of the place a figure has just left
the high byte of the place a figure has just left
the low byte of the sixteen tiles, four by four, a figure is drawn from

the high byte of the sixteen tiles, four by four, a figure is drawn from, always $73, set beside $0A by $636A; $62B9 copies it into the operands of the redraw at $62E2, which reads the tiles from $7300 onwards

a note on the zero page; $0091 itself is not used by the game. The zero page the game works in: $02 and $03 the map address being read or written, which the tile fade at $4CCB also points into the character set at $2000; $04 and $05 the map builder's source, and the tile fade's pointer into its copy at $8000; $06 and $07 the tile grid's place in the map, which the door openers also walk; $08 and $09 the place a figure has just left; $0A and $0B the sixteen tiles a figure is drawn from; $C5 the game's flag for the SPACE key; $FA and $FB the room's own place in the map; $FC and $FD the all-purpose pointer; and $FE and $FF the room's offset in tiles, which the floor-select screen also uses as a second pointer into colour memory ($1BFC).
the game's own flag for the SPACE key, $10 while it is held and 0 when it is not, kept in the byte the KERNAL uses for the last key it saw. $5FCB writes it and the main loop reads it.
zero page the game does not use, left as the KERNAL's tape and screen work space
more zero page the game does not use
the low byte of where the room shown on screen begins in the castle map
the high byte of where the room shown on screen begins
the low byte of the all-purpose pointer: the message being printed, the block being copied, the sprite shapes being cleared
the high byte of that pointer
how far across the floor, in tiles, the room on screen begins; the panel's reading of where the player is adds it
how far down the floor, in tiles, the room on screen begins; the panel's reading of where the player is adds it, and the vertical scrolls step it

the start of page 2. At the hand-over $0200 holds $93, $00, $41 and zeros, and $02A7 to $02FF hold the loader's own code (SEI, LDA #$31, STA $0314 ...). The game overwrites that with its own variables from $02A7 onwards, and $404F clears $02A8 to $02FF at the start of every mission.
which floor the player is on, 0 the basement to 3 the second floor
how many rows of blocks of the floor the builder has built so far: $6A73 starts it at 0, $6BBC adds one after each row, and at $20, thirty-two rows, the floor is done
the message line's fine horizontal scroll, stepped down by 4 each frame; when it wraps the text is shifted a character along

which way the player is crossing into the next room, and how far the scroll has got: the low three bits hold the direction, 1 to 4, and the top four count the scroll's steps ($4329 sets them, $4377 counts them down). The interrupt's player step at $426F, called from $4B86, reads it to run the scroll, and the four scroll routines step it. Bit 3 is kept through every change ($4327, $4384), and while it is set the interrupt skips $426F ($4B7F).
the mask the tiles are faded in through, shifted left and a bit added each pass until every bit is set
how many door keys the player is carrying, in binary-coded decimal; the panel prints it

where the door being opened lies, as an offset from the map address in $06 that the opener at $50F7 uses: 1 when a shot struck the left half of a steel door, tile $49 ($54B5), and 0 when it struck the right half, tile $4A ($54D4), so the opener finds the right half, $4A, either way; and 6 or 0 when the player opens a door with a key ($5097, $50AB)
how far away the door's other half is in the map, from the same place: $80 or $81 for a steel door that was shot ($54D9, $54BA), and $86 or $80 for a door opened with a key ($509C, $50B0)

which of the player's two shots are in the air: bit 0 the first, bit 4 the second. Bit 1 is flipped when the first shot passes the edge of the room and bit 5 likewise for the second, and $4586 then takes that shot out of the air.
the way the player is facing, which is the way a shot goes: 1 up, 2 down, 3 left, 4 right
the way the first shot is travelling, 1 up, 2 down, 3 left, 4 right, taken from the player's facing when it was fired
how many steps the first shot has taken, one a move, each step a tile of 8 pixels; the second shot cannot be fired until this has reached 8 ($4646)
the way the second shot is travelling
how far the second shot has travelled
set while fire is still held, so one press fires one shot
the position across the room a tile lookup is about, in pixels
the position down the room a tile lookup is about, in pixels
the tile code the door opener at $50F7 looks for: $4A when a shot opens a steel door ($54BF, $54DE), and $44 when the player opens a door with a key ($508B)
the tile code the wooden door opener at $5192 looks for: $47 when a shot opens a wooden door ($54F3, $5508), and $45 when it is set at $5146
counts frames 0 to 3; the player may move on the frame it reaches 3, so one step takes four frames
the screen code of the upper digit $5A20 has just made
the screen code of the lower digit $5A20 has just made
how many rounds the player has, kept in binary-coded decimal so the panel can print it a digit at a time. A mission starts with $99, that is 99.

set when "YOU NEED A LIFT PASS !" ($507C) or "THIS DOOR IS LOCKED !" ($50D8) has been printed, so it is not printed again while the player stays where he is. When another message is still on the line, $506C and $50C8 store the message queue's read position $592B here instead, which, unless that is 0, skips the warning rather than keeping it for later. Every step he takes clears it ($4315, $43BD, $4467, $450F). The idle nag at $5A33 does not read it.
how many times $02C1 has filled with the player standing still; at fourteen the game says so
how many turns of $02C1 have passed with fire not held; at seven the game asks for some destruction

counted on each time $5A33 runs, which is in one pass of the interrupt's three-step rota ($4B24), so at most every third frame. It runs round all 256 values, and each time it reaches $80 the nag counters are looked at: $02BF is stepped if the stick is not pushed and no message is showing, and cleared otherwise, and $02C0 likewise with the fire button.
the top two digits of the score, in binary-coded decimal
the middle two digits of the score
the bottom two digits of the score. Nothing ever adds to them, so they stay at zero.

points waiting to be added to the score, a plain binary count: the finds add 25, 15 or 40 at a time with binary ADC ($4EC4, $4EEE, $4F48, $5DA6), shooting a figure adds 25 ($687A, $6904), and $6F26 adds 1. The ticker at $5AA0 takes one a frame with DEC and adds 1 to the middle score digits, so each is worth a hundred.
how many hits the player has taken, in binary-coded decimal. Cold food takes $10 off it, first aid clears it, and the panel prints it.
how many of the end-of-mission slides are left: $6913 makes one slide, then sets this to 10 and makes ten more
what the lift pass has got to: 1 once the player is carrying one, 2 once he has stepped onto the lift with it, which the main loop takes him off the floor for

set while the game is paused, and also once play has stopped: by the game over ($48F2), the lift ($48DA), a delivered prisoner ($49F2), a destroyed castle ($4A62) and the explosives ($55E5). While it is set the interrupt skips the rota of play work ($4AE5) and the sprites ($4B5F); the score ticker, the sound, the mission state and the message line still run.
where the player is in the castle, across, counted in tiles: the position in the room plus the room's own offset
where the player is in the castle, down, counted in tiles
how far through its four-call rota the figures' turn has got, 0 to 3: the call that finds it at 3 puts it back to 0 and starts the list again from the first figure ($6044)
counts the figures that have moved

which figure of the list the figures' turn has reached: each call of $6044 carries on from here, moving up to seven figures, and the list starts again from the first when it reaches $02CF or when $02CC comes round to 3
how many figures the floor's description put on this floor
the tile column, 0 to $7C in steps of 4, of the block the builder is filling in; $6AF4 stores it as a figure's place across
the tile row, 0 to $7C in steps of 4, of the row of blocks the builder is filling in; $6AFA stores it as a figure's place down
the direction the shot that just hit something was travelling, kept so the thing hit knows which way the bullet came
0 while the mission is being played, $FF once the player is dead, and 1 to $12 while the explosives from a chest are going off
how many times the explosion's run of colours has been round; the fifth ends the game

which sound to start, read once a frame by $63F3: 1 to 9, and 0 for none. Firing sets 5, a find 1, as does a shot at a detonator ($539B), a shot at a door key 2 ($53B9), a shot at a locked door ($43 to $46, $5312) 3, healing 4, a door opened with a key 6, the explosives 7, a figure shot 8, and 9 a shot that opens a door or destroys a pickup or a box of ammunition ($53CA to $5522).
which sound effect is in progress, so the tick at $6615 can carry it on
how many frames the sound in progress has left
the lowest bit of the player's step count. Only the sound reads it, which is why a footstep is heard on every other step.
stepped on with each footstep ($67A0), which is every other step of the player; its lowest bit picks one of two pitches, so the footsteps alternate between them
counts the player's steps. After each step its lowest bit is copied to $02D8, which sets off a footstep, and bit 1 picks the walking pose of the player's sprites ($4BBC).
the first shot's position across the room, in pixels
the first shot's position down the room, in pixels
the second shot's position across the room, in pixels
the second shot's position down the room, in pixels
the player's position across the room, in pixels, which the four player sprites are placed from
the player's position down the room, in pixels
how far through the table of random numbers the game has got; it runs round and round the 256 bytes
set to 0 at $5D3B before the search of the sixteen places at $5CA9; nothing reads it, as the search counts in X
set by $46A5 each time a shot is fired and cleared at $42A9 once fire is let go; while it is set the player does not move ($429A) and his walking frames are left alone ($4BB3)
counts to 1 and back, so the prisoner moves on every other call of $6C3B; that runs only in the third pass of the interrupt's three-step rota ($4B04, $5B72), so he moves at most once every six frames

set to 1 at $41C3 when the floor being entered does not have the prisoner on it, either because the mission has none ($4010 = $FF) or because he is on another floor; while it is set $6C3B returns at once and he does not move. Only the clear of page 2 by $404F, at the start of a mission and after each lift ride, puts it back to 0.
the floor the player was on before the lift, kept so the game can tell whether the prisoner was left behind
the tile under the player ($5C42) when the end-of-mission check at $5F27 last looked, so that standing on tile $E4 sets the check off once rather than on every pass

set to 1 when the prisoner's place lies outside the window round the room on screen and cleared when it lies inside, at each of his turns ($6C35, $6C6F); read after a lift ride ($49B5) and by $5F27 to decide whether he was left behind
what the game's own code wants the main loop to do next: 1 when a prisoner has been brought home, 2 when the castle has been destroyed
where in the castle map this floor's dynamite charge is, low byte, taken from the byte $62 in the floor's description
where this floor's dynamite charge is, high byte
where in the castle map the floor's description put the prisoner, low byte; the mission's own copy of his place is in $6029
where the floor's description put the prisoner, high byte

which of the three phases of the interrupt's rota ran last, 1 or 2, or 0 after the third: $4AF1 steps it before choosing, so the heavy work is spread over three frames. While the room scrolls, $4AEF skips the rota and draws the room every frame, and $4278 holds it at 0.
which of the two the stamped-in player is for: 1 runs only the figures, anything else runs the prisoner as well

set once a figure outside the window round the room on screen has moved ($60CB), so only one such figure moves on each pass through the list; cleared when the turn comes round to the end of the list ($609A, $60B5)
the low byte of the interrupt vector, which each of the game's five interrupt handlers is written into in turn
the high byte of the interrupt vector at $0314. The game writes the high byte of each of its five interrupt handlers here, and $EA when it puts the KERNAL's handler back ($15BA, $494E, $4A37, $4A92).
jump stub into the high score check at $0B89, called from the game's own code at $4943 and $4AA3 when a game ends, and from $802E after the reset code has set the score to zeros

the player's score as six ASCII digits, "000000" at the hand-over. $4918 and $4A67 copy it off the panel's digits at $05D7 when a game ends, $4042 and $8024 set it to zeros, and only the high score check ($0BA3) and the table insert ($0D2A) read it.

the name typed on the name-entry screen, ten characters as the big alphabet's six-bit codes (A is 1, the digit 0 is $30), all "." at the hand-over. $0CE7 fills it from the screen, $0D19 copies it into the high score table, and the cheat check at $6F3B compares it.

the offset into the high score table at $0D50 of the entry being looked at: $0B89 starts it at $0D, the first entry's score, and steps it by 20 until $C8; $0BC1 takes $0D off to point at the start of the entry the score beat, which $0CF8 then uses to shift the table down and write the new entry
jump stub into the death screen at $1A21, called from the game at $4931
jump stub into the floor-select screen at $1AB2, called from the game at $499E when the player rides the lift
jump stub into the mission-select screen at $1D23, called from the game at $4966
jump stub into the mission briefing at $1E3F, called from the game at $4A4E

which mission the player chose, 1 to 4, set by the mission-select screen ($1D32, stepped by $1DE4 and $1DF6) and, before the next briefing, copied in at $4A4B from the game's own mission count $400F, which $4A45 has just stepped on; read by the mission select and the briefing ($1EB1, $1EBD)
jump stub into the end-of-mission screen at $1F3C, called from the game at $4AA0

stops CIA 1's timer A, turns the video chip's raster interrupt on, points the interrupt vector $0314 at the handler at $085A, asks for the first interrupt on line 0 and clears the band counter at $0859. Called once, from $0CD9.

which band of the attract screen's raster split the last interrupt served, 0 (the picture) to 3; the handler at $085A steps it before choosing, so the next interrupt serves the band after it, and the picture band puts it back to 0

the attract screens' raster interrupt, a chain of four bands counted by $0859. Band 0 sets the picture at the top ($08A5) and asks for line $78, band 1 the text below it ($08FC) and line $C6, band 2 the scrolling strip's fine position ($0929) and line $DA, band 3 puts the fine position back ($0935) and line 0. Band 0 ends by jumping into the KERNAL's own interrupt handler at $EA31, so the jiffy clock and the keyboard still run; the other three return with RTI.

band 0: multicolour bitmap mode ($D011 = $3B, $D016 = $D8) with video bank 3, so the plaque's bitmap at $E000 and its colours at $EC00 are what the top of the screen shows. Then reads the joystick ($0A13) and redraws the name-entry cursor ($0940).
switches to multicolour text with the screen at $0400 and the character set at $2800, video bank 0, blanking the display for the change ($D011 = $7B, then $1B). Called from $0FB2.

band 1: single-colour text with the screen at $0400 and the character set at $2800, video bank 0, so the words below the picture are drawn from the two-cell-wide alphabet. Blanks the display across the change, as $08D0 does.
the fine horizontal position of the name-entry screen's scrolling alphabet, 0 or 4 in the video chip's own units; band 2 puts it into $D016 and the joystick routines step it by 4
band 2: puts $0928 into the low four bits of $D016, which scrolls the alphabet strip at the bottom of the name-entry screen sideways without redrawing it
band 3: puts the fine horizontal position back to 0 and 40 columns ($D016 low nibble = 8), so only the strip's own band is scrolled

draws the character the name-entry strip has under its pointer at the cursor, row 23, column 10 plus twice the number of characters typed so far ($0CD3). It reads the character from the screen cell $070B, row 19 column 19, the strip's cell under the pointer, and turns the cell's code back into the character by adding 1 and shifting right twice.
set when fire has acted on the name-entry screen ($097D, $09A4) and cleared at $0A31 when none of left, right and fire is held, so one press of fire takes one character
what fire does on the name-entry screen: returns at once while $095D is set, so a held button acts once, and otherwise runs on into $0964

takes the character the strip shows under its pointer, at $070B. Unless it is the alphabet's last character, "_" (code $1F), it steps the cursor on, up to ten characters; "_" instead draws a full stop at the cursor and steps the cursor back one, not below 0. Reached from $095E, which the joystick reader at $0A13 jumps to.
how far the name-entry alphabet strip has scrolled, in half-characters, 0 to $5F; $09AB redraws the strip from it and the joystick steps it
the strip position in whole characters, $09A9 shifted right; $09AB indexes the alphabet at $0B48 with it

redraws the name-entry screen's alphabet strip into rows 19 and 20 ($06F8 and $0720) from the alphabet at $0B48, starting at the character $09A9 names and wrapping at the 48th. On an even half-step it writes each character's four cells in place; on an odd one it writes the right-hand half of one character beside the left-hand half of the next, which is how the strip moves half a character at a time.

reads the joystick on control port 2 ($DC00) for the name-entry screen: left scrolls the alphabet strip one way ($0A37), right the other ($0A5A), fire takes the character under the pointer ($095E), and when none of the three is held it clears the one-press flag $095D. Called once a frame from band 0 of the attract interrupt.

scrolls the name-entry alphabet strip one step right: adds 4 to the fine position, and when that reaches 8 puts it back to 0 and moves the strip back a half-character, wrapping at $5F, then redraws the strip

scrolls the name-entry alphabet strip one step left: takes 4 from the fine position, and when that underflows puts it back to 4 and moves the strip on a half-character, wrapping at $60, then redraws the strip
the top-left cell's code, worked out by the plotter at $0A84
the top-right cell's code
the bottom-left cell's code
the bottom-right cell's code

the character the plotter at $0A84 is to draw, as a six-bit code (A is 1 and the digit 0 is $30). Most callers mask it with AND #$3F; the three at $139E, $13B9 and $13D4 store the ASCII letters as they are, which draws the same because the plotter's two left shifts drop bits 6 and 7.
the column the plotter writes at, 0 to 39, stepped on by 2 after each character
the row the plotter writes at, stepped on by 2 when the column passes 39
the colour the plotter puts in both of the character's upper colour cells
the colour for both of its lower cells

draws one character of the big alphabet, which is two cells wide and two high. Multiplies $0A7F by four for the four cell codes (top-left n, bottom-left n+1, top-right n+2, bottom-right n+3), builds the screen address $0400 + 40 * $0A81 + $0A80 by adding 40 a row at a time, writes the four codes, adds $D4 to the pointer's high byte to reach colour memory at $D800 and writes $0A82 to the upper pair and $0A83 to the lower, then steps the column on by two and the row by two when the column passes 39. 48 places call it.
"     WELL DONE      YOU ARE A REAL HERO ", ASCII ending $FF; drawn as two rows of twenty characters by $0C2A
"  ENTER YOUR NAME", ASCII ending $FF

the 48 characters the name-entry strip offers, ASCII: "@ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ 0123456789!\"#$%&'()_". No end byte follows them: $09AB counts to 48 and wraps, so the strip is endless. The last, "_", is the rubout $0964 tests for.
the name field drawn at row 23 by $0CBE: four spaces, ")", ten full stops where the typed letters go, and "(", ASCII ending $FF

compares the score at $0819, digit by digit as ASCII, with each of the ten entries in the table at $0D51, twenty bytes apart. On the first entry the score beats, it goes to the name entry at $0BC1; on an equal digit it compares the next, and a score equal to an entry's does not beat it; otherwise it steps $0829 on by 20 and tries the next, and when that passes $C8 the score made no entry and it returns to the attract loop at $1014. Blanks the display and banks every ROM in on the way in.

builds the name-entry screen. Takes $0D off $0829 to point at the entry the score beat, copies the colour memory of the plaque at the top from the tables at $EE00 and $EF00 with the KERNAL banked out, clears rows 9 to 24 with the big alphabet's space, sets the strip's position to $4F half-characters, which puts "A" under the pointer, colours rows 8, 19 and 20, and draws the strip and the text. The JSR at $0CD9 then installs the attract interrupt, and it waits for ten characters.

draws the text of the name-entry screen through the plotter at $0A84, run on into from the strip draw at $0C27 rather than called: "WELL DONE / YOU ARE A REAL HERO" from $0B0D at row 9, adding a row and a column after its first twenty characters so the second half starts at row 12, column 1; "ENTER YOUR NAME" from $0B36 at row 16; the pointer, character $1E, at row 21 column 19, whose lower half $0CA2 rubs out; and the name field from $0B78 at row 23. Each has its own pair of colours.
how many characters of the name have been typed, 0 to 10; the name-entry screen waits for it to reach 10, and fire steps it
clears the count of characters typed and installs the attract interrupt, then waits for the name to be finished
spins until ten characters have been typed, with the attract interrupt doing the work: the strip, the cursor and the joystick are all handled by band 0
reads the ten typed characters back off the screen itself, from row 23 at $07A3 taking every other cell, shifts each right twice to undo the plotter's multiply by four, and leaves them in $081F

makes room for the new entry by copying the table down twenty bytes, from the end back to the place the score beat, then fills the entry with spaces, the name from $081F and the score from $0819. The source address $0D3C is simply $0D50 less twenty; the bytes there are a delay loop, not a table.

a counted delay of 846,856 cycles, about 0.86 seconds, that holds a blank screen ($D011 = $7B, set just before) once the new entry is in the table, with the interrupts off since the SEI at $0D36, so no music plays; then the attract loop starts again at $1014. Three loops deep: X and Y count 255 each, and the innermost counts A down from 1, so it runs once a turn. The shift at $0CF8 reads these same bytes as its source, which is only how it addresses the table twenty bytes lower.
the space before the first high score entry's name; the ten entries run from here, twenty bytes apart

the high score table: ten entries of 20 bytes from $0D50, each a space, a ten-character name, two spaces, a six-digit score and a space. The shipped names are PANDORA and three spaces and the scores ASCII; a name typed in goes in as six-bit codes.
the first entry's score, six ASCII digits; every entry is twenty bytes, so the scores are twenty bytes apart
the rest of the ten high score entries, from inside the fourth entry's score; each entry is a space, a ten-character name, two spaces, a six-digit score and a space
nineteen spaces before the high score table's heading. No instruction reads them: the heading itself starts at $0E2C.
the high score table's heading, " TODAYS REAL HEROES" with a space before it, ASCII ending $FF at $0E3F. $106C reads it from here.

installs the title screen's fade interrupt: blanks the display, black border and background, stops CIA 1's timer A, points $0314 at $0E6A, asks for line 0 and turns the raster interrupt on. Called from the title screen builder at $1024.

the title screen's raster interrupt: a fade worked by rewriting colour memory. $1012 says which phase it is in (0 fade in, 2 fade out, 3 hold, 1 and 4 idle), $1011 the step inside it, 0 to 9. Each step takes four colours from the tables at $0FE5, $0FEF, $0FF9 and $1003, puts them in $100D to $1010 and calls $0EF9 to paint the four bands of the screen with them. The fade in counts up to 10 and goes to the hold, the hold counts $1013 to 256 and starts the fade out, the fade out counts down to 0 and stops. It then calls the music at $1947 and ends through the KERNAL's handler at $EA31.

paints the four bands of the title screen with the four colours in $100D to $1010. The first two bands are one row each, rows 0 and 1 of colour memory, under the heading; the third is the ten odd rows 3 to 21 from $D878 and the fourth the ten even rows 4 to 22 from $D8A0, the upper and lower halves of the high score table's letters. Rows 2, 23 and 24 are never written. Called by both halves of the fade.

installs the interrupt the credits, supplies and valuables screens run on. Banks every ROM in, blanks the display, copies the plaque's colour memory from $EE00 and $EF00 with the KERNAL banked out, stops CIA 1's timer A, clears the band flag $0F94, points $0314 at $0F95 and asks for line 0. Called from $11C8.
which band the plaque screens' interrupt served last, flipped at the start of each one: after the flip 0 draws the picture at the top and 1 the text below it

the interrupt the credits, supplies and valuables screens run on, two bands flipped by $0F94. On the picture band it switches to the bitmap ($0FC0), asks for line $78 and plays the music at $1947, ending through the KERNAL's handler at $EA31; on the text band it switches back to text ($08D0), asks for line 0 and returns with RTI.
switches the top of the screen to the multicolour bitmap of the stone plaque: bitmap mode, white background 0, video bank 3 and $D018 = $B8, so the bitmap is at $E000 and its colours at $EC00
the first band's colour for each of the ten fade steps
the second band's colour for each step
the third band's colour for each step
the fourth band's colour for each step
the colour the fade's current step gives the first band of the title screen
the second band's colour for this step
the third band's colour for this step
the fourth band's colour for this step
which of the ten steps of the title screen's fade is showing, an index into the four colour tables at $0FE5
which phase the title screen's fade is in: 0 fades in, 2 fades out, 3 holds the picture, 1 and 4 leave it alone
counts the frames the finished title picture is held, from 0 round to 0 again, which is 256 frames, about five seconds on a PAL machine

builds the title screen. the music, one tick at a time, called once a frame from the title and plaque interrupts. It does nothing on two frames in three, so the tune runs at about 16.7 ticks a second on a PAL machine. On the third it serves each of the three voices in turn: it counts the voice's note down, and when that runs out takes the next note number from the voice's own stream ($15E2, $1680 or $1768), looks the number up in the three note tables to get the frequency high byte, the low byte and the length, writes the frequency and the waveform to that voice, and steps the stream on. When the first voice's note number is $FF the tune has ended: the driver sets all three streams back to their beginning and serves the three voices again from the first, in the same tick, so the music is endless. The test at $199E reads the first voice's note whichever voice is being served, so a $FF taken by the second or third voice is not an end: it is looked up in the note tables like any other number.

the player's part of each frame. The low three bits of $02AA say what is going on: 1, 2, 3 or 4 means a room change is in progress and the matching scroll runs a step of it ($432E up, $43D6 down, $4480 left, $4528 right); with none of them set the player takes an ordinary turn at $4297.

the player's turn, once a frame. It works out which tiles are round the player ($5C46), holds everything until fire is let go when $02E3 says a shot is pending, and then counts $02BA up to 3 and acts only on the fourth frame, which is why the player steps one tile every four frames. On that frame it reads control port 2 and goes to the routine for the direction pushed: up $42E2, down $438A, left $4434, right $44DC.

moves the player up a tile when nothing solid is in the way. The four tiles round the player, which $5C46 left in $5C23 to $5C26, must all be below $2D: a tile code of $2D or more is a wall, a door or furniture and stops the move. Otherwise it takes 8 from the player's y, clears $02BE, so a "THIS DOOR IS LOCKED !" or "YOU NEED A LIFT PASS !" warning can be printed again, counts the step in $02DA, whose bit 1 picks the walking pose, and copies its lowest bit to $02D8 for the footstep. At y = $62 the player is at the top edge of the room, so instead it asks for the room above by setting bits in $02AA.
moves the picture one row at a time while the player crosses into the room above, ten steps counted the same way as $43D6 counts the downward crossing
moves the player down a tile when the four tiles at $5C41 to $5C44 are all below $2D. At y = $B2 the player is at the bottom edge, so it asks for the room below instead by setting bits in $02AA.

moves the picture one row at a time while the player crosses into the room below, ten steps counted in the top nibble of $02AA, which the edge set to $A. Each step moves the room pointer in $FA on by 128 bytes, takes 8 off the player's y, and brings each shot in the air with it, so a bullet keeps its place in the room rather than on the screen. The last step keeps only bit 3 of $02AA, which nothing sets, so $02AA ends at 0; $4B82 tests that bit and skips the player's part while it is set.

moves the player left a tile when the four tiles at $5C28, $5C2E, $5C34 and $5C3A are all below $2D, and sets the facing to 3. At x = $48 the player is at the left edge, so it asks for the room to the left instead.

moves the picture one column at a time while the player crosses into the room on the left, thirteen steps counted in the top nibble of $02AA, which the edge set to $D. Each step decrements the room's column offset in $FE, moves the room pointer in $FA back a byte, adds 8 to the player's x, and brings each shot in the air with it; when $FE is already 0 the step only moves the player and ends the crossing.

moves the player right a tile when the four tiles at $5C2D, $5C33, $5C39 and $5C3F are all below $2D, and sets the facing to 4. At x = $B0 the player is at the right edge, so it asks for the room to the right instead.

moves the picture one column at a time while the player crosses into the room on the right, thirteen steps counted in the top nibble of $02AA, which the edge set to $D. The mirror of $4480: $FE counts up and ends the crossing at $64, the room pointer goes on a byte, the player's x comes back 8, and the shots in the air come with it.

takes a shot out of the air once it has passed a room's edge, which is what bits 1 and 5 of $02AF mark, one shot a call, and then goes on to the fire routine at $45BD, which runs whatever is still flying ($4692)

fire. It moves the shots already in the air ($4692) and then, if fire is held and this is a fresh press, fires one. The player can have two shots in the air at once: a new one is fired when neither is, or once the one in the air has taken 8 steps of 8 pixels. With no rounds left it says "OUT OF AMMO!"; otherwise it takes one off the ammunition in decimal mode, points the player's sprites the right way ($46A5), asks for sound effect 5, and starts the shot from the player's own position offset by the tables at $4699 and $469D.

fires the player's second shot, once the first has taken at least 8 steps of 8 pixels and no second one is already in the air. It spends a round, points the sprites, asks for sound effect 5, and starts the shot at the player.
moves each of the player's two shots along one step; the interrupt reaches it through $4586 on two frames in three, and not during a pause or a room change
how far across the player the shot starts, one byte for each of the four directions
how far down the player the shot starts, one byte for each of the four directions

moves the player's first shot 8 pixels in its direction, if one is in the air, and counts the step in $02B2. When the new position is past the edge of the room (below $3A at the top, $E2 or more at the bottom, below $20 at the left, $F2 or more at the right) it flips bit 1 of $02AF, which $4586 reads to take the shot out. Any direction other than 1 to 3 moves it right.

moves the player's second shot one tile in its direction, the same way as $46FA does the first, except that it flips bit 5 of $02AF rather than bit 1 and its right edge is $F0. It counts $02B4 up on every call, before it tests whether a second shot is in the air.
the rows of the room left to draw, less one: set to 20 and counted down past 0, so 21 rows are drawn

draws the whole room, 28 tiles across and 21 rows down, from the castle map the pointer in $FA names. It is written as a self-modifying loop: the bytes at $4815, $4818 and $481E are the operands of the three instructions in the inner loop, holding the map address, the screen address and the colour address, and the routine rewrites them as it goes. Each tile code goes to the screen and the colour the tile colour table at $8600 gives it goes to colour memory. A row of the map is 128 bytes, so each row adds $80 to the source and 40 to the two destinations.
the operand of the instruction that reads the map: the address of the row being drawn
the high byte of the map address the room drawer reads, which it steps on every second row, when adding $80 to the low byte wraps it to $00
the operand of the instruction that writes the screen
the high byte of the screen address the room drawer writes, which it steps on when adding 40 to the low byte carries
the operand of the instruction that writes colour memory

the high byte of the colour-memory address the room drawer writes, the second byte of the operand of the STA at $481D. $47F1 sets it to $D8 at $4800 and $4841 steps it on when the row's low byte carries.

hands the machine over to the game: points $0314 at the game's own interrupt at $4AA7, stops CIA 1's timer A, asks for a raster interrupt on line $E9, banks BASIC out and leaves the KERNAL and the I/O in ($01 = $36), and drops into the loop at $4871

the game's main loop, which does nothing itself but watch four things and hand over when one of them happens. $02D3 = $FF means the player is dead or the explosives in a chest have been shot ($48F0), $02C8 = 2 that he has stepped onto the lift ($48D4), $02E9 = 1 that a prisoner has been brought home ($49EC) and 2 that the castle has been destroyed ($4A5C), and $C5 = $10 that SPACE is down, which pauses. Everything else - the player, the guards, the shots, the panel - is done by the interrupt.

SPACE pauses. It sets the pause flag, waits for SPACE to be let go, and then holds the game: with nothing on the joystick and the message line idle it prints "...PAUSING...", and it keeps printing it until SPACE or the stick is touched, when it clears the flag and the loop goes on.

the player has stepped onto the lift carrying a pass. It writes $26 to $01 (the same banking as play: BASIC out, KERNAL and I/O in), sets the pause flag, holds the game while the message line empties, turns every sprite off, slides the room away ($6018) and goes to $4946, which asks which floor to ride to.

the player is dead, or the explosives in a chest have been shot. It sets the pause flag, redraws the panel's numbers ($5995), waits for the message line to empty, waits ($5FDA), silences all three voices and the volume, turns the sprites off, copies the six score digits off the panel at $05D7 into $0819 as ASCII for the high score check, slides the room away ($6018), blanks the screen ($D011 = $6B), shows "YOU ARE DEAD" ($082A, which goes to $1A21), banks BASIC back in ($01 = $37) and goes to the high score check at $0810.

what happens between missions. Points $0314 at $EA34 in the KERNAL's interrupt handler, turns the raster interrupt off and starts CIA 1's timer A again, so the mission screens have a working keyboard. With no mission in progress it clears $4012 (the prisoner rode the lift) and asks for a mission ($1D23): mission 1 puts the prisoner in the basement, 2 on the first floor, 3 on the second, and 4, the demolition, has no prisoner, which is $FF in $4010. With a mission already in progress it asks which floor the lift should go to ($1AB2) instead, takes the prisoner along when he was on the floor left behind and $02E8 is clear, and keeps the keys, the ammunition, the hits and the three bytes of the score in $4009 to $400E while the screens are up.

a prisoner has been brought home. It waits for the message line to empty, then sets up the next mission's start: no keys, the ammunition back to 99 and the hits to none, and the score kept ($4009 to $400E). It clears $6043 and $4012, slides the room away ($6018), puts the KERNAL's interrupt back ($EA34), counts the mission on in $400F and copies it to $0836, shows the next mission's briefing ($0833), sets $4011 so that $5EE2 starts the player as for a new mission, and goes back to $496C to start it.

the castle has been destroyed. It copies the six score digits off the panel into $0819, waits for the message line to empty, slides the room away, puts the KERNAL's interrupt back and shows the end-of-mission screen ($0837), then goes to the high score check at $0810.
which of the game's two interrupt bands comes next, flipped between 1 and 0 each time

the game's own interrupt, and where nearly everything in play happens. It serves two bands, flipped by $4AA6: one sets the screen to the play character set at $2000 and does the game's work ($4ACD), then asks for line $E3; the other sets the message line's character set at $2800 with its fine scroll and draws the sprites ($4B4C), then asks for line $FC. It never chains to the KERNAL's handler, so the jiffy clock and the KERNAL's keyboard scan do not run while the game is playing, which is why the game scans SPACE itself.

the interrupt's first band. Puts the screen on the play character set at $2000 in multicolour with 38 columns, adds a waiting point to the score ($5AA0), redraws the panel's numbers ($5995) unless $02EF is 0, and scans SPACE ($5FCB). Unless the game is paused it then does one of two things. While a room change is under way (the low three bits of $02AA) it redraws the room ($47F1). Otherwise it steps a three-phase rota counted in $02EF: phase 1 redraws the room ($47F1); phase 2 runs the walked-onto test ($4D3A), the shots ($5212, $4586), the prodding ($5A33), the player's stamp with only the figures ($5B1B with $02F0 = 1), the jewels ($5CB9) and the end-of-mission check ($5F27); phase 3 puts $02EF back to 0 and runs the shots ($5212, $4586) and the stamp with the prisoner as well ($02F0 = 3). Every path ends by stepping the message line's scroll ($4B35).

steps the message line four pixels left, and when two steps have used up a whole cell shifts the line's text one cell along ($4BDC) and brings the next cell in ($5951). A character of the big alphabet is two cells wide, so it takes four steps.

the interrupt's second band. Puts the screen on the big alphabet at $2800 with the message line's fine scroll in $D016, runs the sound's frame ($600C, which goes to $63E6) and checks the hits and steps the explosion ($5BBA). Unless the game is paused it counts the flash at the barrel down after a shot is fired, turning sprite 4 yellow at 2 and parking it at (0,0) at 0, and runs the player and the room changes ($426F) unless bit 3 of $02AA is set, which nothing in the code sets: the mission start clears it ($4058) and the room changes only keep it. It then places the player's four sprites round the position in $02DF and $02E0 and, unless a shot is pending ($02E3), sets their shape pointers at $07F8 to $07FB from the direction ($02B0), the table at $4BD8 and bit 1 of the step count $02DA.

the first sprite shape of the player's walking pose for each direction: $C0 up, $C4 down, $C8 left, $CC right. $4BC4 reads it with the direction less one and adds $10 while bit 1 of the step count $02DA is set, so the pose changes after every two steps.
shifts the message line's two rows one cell to the left, so the text moves on after the fine scroll has used up a whole cell
the raster line the wipe's open band starts at
the raster line the wipe's open band ends at
which of the wipe interrupt's two bands comes next, flipped each time

how far the wipe at the start of play has got. $4BF2 leaves it at 0, which closes the window, and the interrupt answers 3 when it has closed ($4095 waits for that). The main code then sets 1 to open it again ($4239), and the interrupt answers 2 when it is open ($4241 waits for that).

installs the interrupt that wipes the screen shut and open again when play starts on a floor ($4092): stops CIA 1's timer A, turns the raster interrupt on, sets the band to lines $32 to $FA, sets $4BF1 to 0 and points $0314 at $4C22

the interrupt that opens and shuts the screen. Its two bands set the display on inside the band and an invalid, black mode outside it, so what shows is a window that closes to the middle of the screen and opens again four lines at a time. It reports where it has got to in $4BF1.

the band outside the window: an invalid video mode, which the chip draws as black, and the player's sprites turned black with it. It is also where the window's two lines are moved, four at a time, towards the middle of the screen and back out again.
the band inside the window: text with the display on ($D011 = $1B), and the player's sprites in their own colours, yellow with black and green shared

would fade the room in, but nothing calls it. It copies the whole play character set out to $8000 and clears it, so every tile is blank, then copies it back eight times through a mask that grows a bit at a time from bit 0 - 1, 3, 7 and so on to $FF - so each character fills in from its right-hand edge one bit column at a time. $02AB is the mask.
the sixteen places in the tile grid that the player's own square covers, rows 1 to 4 and columns 1 to 4, which $4D3A tests first for a tile with any bit of $38 set

looks through the tile grid for anything the player has walked onto. It first tests the sixteen places his own square covers ($4D2A) for a tile with any bit of $38 set; with none it writes the grid back and goes on to the lift and door checks at $5040. Otherwise it scans the grid's first five rows and columns for the first tile of an object: a door key ($10) is counted and named, a painting ($14), a vase ($18), cold food ($1C), a pendant ($28), first aid ($20) and a lift pass ($08) are each picked up by their own routine, and a box of ammunition ($12) anywhere but the grid's top row gives ammunition ($4F62).
the player walked onto a door key: counts it in decimal mode, says "YOU HAVE FOUND" and "A DOOR KEY.", and clears its two tiles
writes the six-by-six grid of tiles back into the castle map, so that whatever a pickup or a shot changed in the grid reaches the map and then the screen
the player walked onto a painting: says "YOU HAVE FOUND", puts 25 points in the queue, which the ticker turns into 2500, and falls into the shared tail that names it
clears the painting from the map, says "A PAINTING." and redraws the room's tiles
the player walked onto a vase: "YOU HAVE FOUND" and 15 waiting points, which is 1500
clears the vase from the map, says "A VASE." and redraws
the player walked onto cold food: "YOU HAVE FOUND", and takes $10 off the hits in decimal mode, stopping at none
clears the food from the map, says "SOME COLD FOOD." and redraws
the player walked onto a pendant: "YOU HAVE FOUND" and 40 waiting points, which is 4000
clears the pendant from the map, says "A PENDANT." and redraws

the player walked onto a box of ammunition, tile $12. It clears the box's two tiles from the grid and adds $10 to the ammunition in decimal mode, which is ten rounds; if that would carry past 99, which it does from 90 up, it sets 99 instead and, when the message line is idle, says "ANY MORE AMMO WOULD BE WASTED !". A pickup that fits says nothing and asks for no sound.

the high byte of the operand of the STA $5C22,Y at $4F68, which clears the box's second tile. Nothing refers to this byte; the part of the pickup that runs when the count would carry past 99 starts at $4F74.
the player walked onto first aid: "YOU HAVE FOUND", and clears the hits altogether

works out the map address one tile left of the place the first aid was found at in the tile grid (the grid's corner plus a row of 128 for each six places and the column, less one; when the column's addition carries, $4FCC decrements the high byte where it should increment it). It clears the object's two-by-two square in the grid ($502A), writes the grid back, then clears five more map tiles from that address: the one left of each of the square's two rows and three on the row below. Then it says "FIRST AID.". Nothing is scored.

the player walked onto a lift pass: "YOU HAVE FOUND", clears the one grid place the scan found it at (only that tile, where the other pickups clear two or four), says "A LIFT PASS." and marks the pass as carried in $02C8
rubs an object out of the tile grid, which the redraw then takes to the screen

reached from $4D3A when the player has walked onto nothing. If the tile just below his square in the grid's third column ($5C42) is $54 or $55, the lift: with a pass ($02C8 not zero) it sets $02C8 to 2, which the main loop takes him off the floor for, and says "YOU ARE ENTERING THE LIFT."; without one it says "YOU NEED A LIFT PASS !" when the message line is idle, the frame counter $02BA (0 to 3) is not 0 and $02BE is clear, and sets $02BE. Otherwise it goes on at $508B to the doors a key opens: $43 to his right ($5C33) or $44 to his left ($5C2E), which $50F7 opens, and $45 below him ($5C42) or $46 above ($5C24), which $5192 opens. With a key in hand it takes one off in decimal mode and asks for sound 6; without one it says "THIS DOOR IS LOCKED !" on the same conditions as the lift message.

works out where in the castle map a place on the screen is. The room's top left corner is x = $20, y = $3A, a tile is eight pixels square and a row of the map is 128 bytes, so the address is the room pointer in $FA plus 16 times the pixels down plus an eighth of the pixels across. It leaves the address in $02 and $03.

looks up the map tile each shot in the air has reached. Tiles $3E and $3F and the codes below $08 are air, so the shot flies on; anything else stops it. On a hit the shot is taken out of the air, its direction is kept in $02D2 and $529B decides what was hit.

decides what a shot hit, by the tile code. $76 to $C0 are the figures ($6040), $D4 to $E3 the prisoner ($6021), and $30 to $3E, $C1 to $CB and $E7 to $EE go to $6015 (the routine at $67FD), which turns some of them into other tiles for 25 points and sound 8 and leaves the rest alone. $5E to $6D are a chest, $49 and $4A the two halves of a steel door, $47 and $48 a wooden door, and $43 to $46, the doors a key opens, only ask for sound 3. Anything else from $40 to $FB goes to the furniture at $542F. The rest is looked for in the six-by-six grid round the shot, where the nine places listed at $5374 are checked for the code of a pickup or of a detonator ($FC).
the nine places in the six-by-six tile grid a shot looks at to find what it hit, since an object is drawn from several tiles and only its first one names it

a shot has set a detonator off: says "DETONATOR ACTIVATED.", marks this floor's charge as armed in $5F9A plus the floor, asks for sound 1, clears the detonator's two-by-two square from the grid and writes the grid back. Nothing is scored.

the shot hit a door key, tile $10. When the message line is idle it says "YOU ARE WAISTING AMMO." (the game's own spelling); it asks for sound 2 and goes to $4DF7, which pushes the key the way the shot was going ($02D2) and writes the grid back. Up or down (1, 2) it moves the key's two tiles a grid row, when both places there are empty; right (4, or any other value) it moves them one tile on, when the place beyond the key is empty. Left (3) is not a move: when the map tile two left of the shot's own place ($02, $03), which is outside the grid, is empty, it writes $10 there in the map and, in the grid, $11 over the key's first tile and 0 over its second, so the key is left broken in two.
a shot hit a box of ammunition, tile $12. It clears the box's two tiles from the grid, asks for sound 9 and writes the grid back to the map at $4E77: the rounds are lost and nothing is scored.

the shot hit a painting: says "YOU HAVE SHOT", asks for sound 9 and goes to $4ECD, which clears it and says "A PAINTING.". No points are queued: the 25 are added only at $4EB4, when it is walked onto.
the shot hit cold food; $4F27 names it and clears it
the shot hit a pendant; $4F51 names it and clears it
the shot hit a vase; $4EF7 names it and clears it
the shot hit first aid; $4FA5 names it and clears it

the shot hit furniture. $4C to $4F are the four tiles of a piece, top left, top right, bottom left and bottom right; whichever was hit, the piece is turned into the broken shape $50 to $53, two tiles on the top row and two on the row below. A shot at the broken shape clears it from the grid. Any other code reaching here is left alone.
the shot hit a lift pass, which is no use at all: "SHOOTING A LIFT PASS IS A BIT SILLY !"

a shot hit the left half of a steel door, code $49. It sets the column offsets $02AD and $02AE to $01 and $81 and the tile to look for to $4A, the right half, takes the shot's map address, asks for sound 9 and opens the door at $50F7, which climbs the right-hand column to the door's top and rewrites the door's tiles.
a shot hit the right half of a steel door, code $4A, and opens it the same way, from the hit tile itself
a shot hit the upper half of a wooden door, code $47, which can be shot open: $5192 does it, clearing the door's two rows
a shot hit the lower half of a wooden door, code $48; the same as $54F3 with the map address moved up a row onto the $47 above

a shot hit a chest, codes $5E to $6D. The code names which of the chest's four tiles was hit, and the routine works back to the chest's own corner and reads its state there: a closed chest ($5E to $61) is opened at $5598, jewels showing ($66 to $69) are wasted at $55F0, and explosives showing ($6A to $6D) go off at $55D5.

opens a closed chest that has been shot. It takes a random number, and only one in four is $C0 or more; on that it takes the next one and opens the chest on jewels ($66) when it is $80 or more and on explosives ($6A) otherwise. The two are neighbouring bytes of the table, which the noise makes alike ($67CA), so the second is $80 or more more often than not: on a C64 with its sound chip running, about one shot in seven shows jewels and one in ten explosives. The other three times in four it says "EMPTY!" and leaves the chest open and empty at $55BB. Nothing else happens on this shot: jewels are taken by walking into them ($5CB9), and explosives go off only when they are shot.
writes the four tiles of an opened chest, $62 to $65, over the chest's own square

a shot hit the explosives in an open chest. It says "FOOL!....EXPLOSIVES.", sets $02D3 to 1, which starts the explosion that ends the game, sets $02C9 and asks for sound 7, which nothing else asks for. Walking into the explosives does nothing.
a shot hit the jewels in an open chest. It says "YOU HAVE SHOT" and "SOME JEWELS." and leaves the chest empty, with no points: the jewels are worth something only walked into ($5CB9).
the game's 33 messages for the line at the bottom of the screen, ASCII, each ending "@" ($40); facts.md lists them
how far the message line's scroll has read into the buffer at $8800
how far the printer has filled the buffer; the line is idle when the two are equal
which half of the character now entering the line is showing, because a character of the big alphabet is two cells wide and the line brings one cell in at a time

puts a message in the queue for the line at the bottom of the screen. $FC and $FD point at the text, which is ASCII ending "@". It copies the characters into the buffer at $8800, masking each to six bits as the big alphabet needs, adds a space after the last, and leaves the write position in $592C. During play the line is emptied only by the scroll ($5991), so a routine that wants to wait for the message to finish watches $592B against $592C; the mission start sets both to 0 ($40A0).

brings the next cell of the message into the right-hand end of the line, at $07BF and $07E7. A character takes two turns, its left half and then its right, after which the read position moves on. With nothing left to show it puts a space there instead.

writes every number on the status panel: the keys at row 4, the ammunition at row 6, the hits at row 8 and the six digits of the score at row 11, each as two screen codes from $5A20. On the way it also works out where the player is in the castle, in tiles, and leaves it in $02CA and $02CB.

turns one binary-coded-decimal byte into the two screen codes that print it. The play character set keeps its digits at $F0 to $F9, so each nibble only has to be ORed with $F0; the upper one is shifted down first. Every number on the panel goes through here.

the game's prodding, run on phase 2 of the rota at $4ACD, one frame in three. $02C1 is stepped on each call, and the counters below act when it reaches $80, which after the first time is once every 256 calls, because $5A3E stores the $80 back rather than clearing it. On such a turn, with no direction pushed and the message line idle, $02BF counts up, and at fourteen the game says "COME ON ! GET ON WITH IT....."; then, with fire not pressed and the line idle, $02C0 counts up, and at seven it says "LETS GET DOWN TO SOME SERIOUS DESTRUCTION !". Each counter is cleared when its message is said, and on such a turn by a busy message line; $02BF also by a push on the stick, and $02C0 by a press of fire.

adds the points waiting in $02C5 to the score, one a frame, so the number on the panel climbs rather than jumps. Each one adds 1 to the score's middle pair of digits in decimal mode, carrying into the top pair, so one waiting point is a hundred on the panel. Nothing adds to the bottom pair: it is only cleared at the mission start ($4058) and copied back from its own saved copy ($4089), which is why every score in this game ends in two zeros.

says which floor the player is on when play starts on a floor, at the start of a mission and after each lift ride ($4268): "YOU ARE" and then one of "IN THE BASEMENT.", "ON THE GROUND FLOOR.", "ON THE FIRST FLOOR." or "ON THE SECOND FLOOR."
the first four of the sixteen tiles the player's square is covering, kept while tile $55 stands in for him
the second four of them
the third four of them
the last four of them

writes the player into the castle map so that the figures can see him. It stamps tile $55 over the sixteen tiles the player's square covers, keeping what was there in the four buffers at $5B0B, $5B0F, $5B13 and $5B17, then runs the figures ($6000) and, unless $02F0 is 1, the prisoner before them ($601E), and puts the sixteen tiles back. With the cheat on ($603F) it then fills the ammunition back to 99. A figure that finds the tile ahead taken compares it with $55 ($6193, $61DC, $6228, $6274) and hits the player on a match, so this is how walking into the player is noticed at all.

watched each frame. While $02D3 is 0 it reads the hits: at $50 or more, that is fifty, the player is dead and $02D3 becomes $FF; below that, with the cheat on ($603F), it sets the keys to 1. $FF means the game is over and the screen goes black. Anything from 1 to $12 is a step of the explosion the explosives from a chest make, which walks the border and the background through the colours at $5C11 and goes round five times before setting $02D3 to $FF. The last step reads one byte past the table, which is the first byte of the tile grid at $5C22.
the seventeen border and background colours the explosives from a chest flash through, in order. The explosion takes eighteen steps, so the last one reads the byte after the table.

the six-by-six block of map tiles read by $5C55 round a place in the map: round the player ($5C46), whose square is the middle four by four, or round where a shot stopped ($5323, $5430). Each move tests the four tiles just outside the player's square on the side he moves to: $5C23 to $5C26 up, $5C41 to $5C44 down, $5C28, $5C2E, $5C34 and $5C3A left, and $5C2D, $5C33, $5C39 and $5C3F right.
the second tile of the grid's first row, and the first of the four tiles just above the player's square, which the move up tests ($42E7)
the second of the four tiles just above the player's square, which the move up, the key door test at $5164 and the jewels at $5CC0 read
the third of the four tiles just above the player's square
the fourth of the four tiles just above the player's square
the last tile of the grid's first row
the second row of the six-by-six tile grid around the player
the right-hand tile of the grid's second row, which the move to the right tests
the third row of the grid
the right-hand tile of the grid's third row
the fourth row of the grid
the right-hand tile of the grid's fourth row
the fifth row of the grid
the right-hand tile of the grid's fifth row
the grid's sixth row
the second tile of the grid's sixth row, which the move down tests
the third tile of the grid's sixth row
the fourth tile of the grid's sixth row
the last two tiles of the six-by-six grid around the player
works out which tiles surround the player, from the position in $02DF and $02E0, by way of $51CD and $5C55, and leaves them in the grid at $5C22

reads the six-by-six block of map tiles round the place whose map address is in $02 and $03 into the grid at $5C22, six bytes a row. It sets $06 and $07 to that address less $81, one row up and one column left, and leaves them there, so the place itself is grid place 7. A row of the map is 128 bytes away, which the routine reaches by setting bit 7 of Y and stepping the pointer's high byte, so it never needs a second pointer.
the sixteen places in the tile grid the jewels are looked for in

the jewels in an opened chest, tiles $66 to $69, taken by walking into them. On phase 2 of the rota at $4ACD, one frame in three, it looks at the two tiles ahead of the player in the first direction the stick is pushed, tested up, down, left, right, and on jewels it works back to the chest's own corner, adds 40 points, which the ticker turns into 4000, says "YOU HAVE FOUND" and "SOME JEWELS.", and leaves the chest open and empty by writing the tiles $62 to $65 over it. Explosives ($6A to $6D) are not looked for, so walking into them does nothing.

draws the status panel: its frame down the right of the screen, the three labels KEYS, AMMO and HITS placed cell by cell from the ten letters the play character set holds, the box round each number, and the colours of every part. It is written with self-modifying operands, as the room drawer is: the screen address at $5DE6 and $5DE7, the colour value at $5DE9 and the colour address at $5DEB and $5DEC.
the low byte of the screen address the panel drawing writes, which $5DC8 rewrites a row at a time
the high byte of the screen address the panel drawing writes, which $5DC8 rewrites
the colour the panel drawing writes to colour memory, the operand of the LDA at $5DE8: $5DE0 sets $0F for the first cell of each row and $5DEF puts $07 back for the rest
the low byte of the colour address the panel drawing writes, the operand of the STA at $5DEA: $5DCD sets it to $45 and $5E02 moves it on with the screen address, a row at a time
the high byte of the colour address the panel drawing writes: $5DD5 sets it to $D8 and $5E0A steps it on when the row's low byte carries

puts the player where the mission starts. Coming out of the lift onto a new floor he is placed at the lift's own square, with the room pointer at $C580; otherwise he starts in the storage room the briefing describes, with the room pointer at $C5B8 and the room's offset in $FE and $FF.

asks whether the mission's job is done, and it is the routine that ends a mission. The test is the tile just below the player's square in the grid's third column ($5C42), which must read $E4; $02E7 keeps it so the test acts once for each arrival rather than on every pass. On the demolition mission, which is the one with no prisoner ($4010 = $FF), all four floors' charges must have been armed, and then it says "THE CASTLE IS NOW DESTROYED." and asks the main loop for $4A5C. On a rescue mission the prisoner must be on this floor ($4010) and close by ($02E8 clear), and then it says "WELL DONE.....YOU HAVE RESCUED A PRISONER." and asks for $49EC. With the job not done it says "YOUR MISSION IS NOT YET COMPLETE !" when the message line is idle, and nothing else happens. Tile $E4 is the way out: it is found only on the ground floor (floor 1), a gap of nineteen in the outer wall on the map's last row ($CFBC to $CFCE). All three outcomes were seen in the emulator with $E4 written under the player (work/t_e4_ground.py).

one byte a floor, in the order basement, ground, first, second, set to 1 once that floor's charge has been armed ($5396). The demolition mission can end only when all four are set, and then only when the player reaches tile $E4 ($5F27).
whether the ground floor's charge has been armed
whether the first floor's charge has been armed
whether the second floor's charge has been armed, the last of the four the demolition mission needs

decides whether this floor's dynamite charge is on the map.
